---
title: "Compatibility"
---

chameleon-rs's goal is to produce exactly what Chameleon produces, for every template, and
to raise the same errors. This page says how that's measured, and lists the few places where
chameleon-rs knowingly differs.

## How it's measured

Each level is a check that runs on every change:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| **Chameleon's own test suite.** All 233 tests, vendored unmodified, run against chameleon-rs. | Every test that passes on Chameleon passes on chameleon-rs: 227 of 227. The other 6 depend on the test environment and are skipped on both engines. |
| **Fixture renders.** Every input template in Chameleon's test suite, rendered by both engines. | All 122 byte-identical. |
| **Differential fuzzing.** Generated templates, models and expressions, rendered by both engines and compared. | No differences in 20,000 examples per generator. |
| **Integration suites.** The test suites of fastapi-chameleon, chameleon-flask, chameleon-robyn, chameleon_partials, litestar-chameleon and pyramid_chameleon, unmodified, on chameleon-rs. | All pass. |
| **Real sites.** Every page of two production Flask/Quart apps, crawled with both engines: anonymous and signed in, with all their partials and layouts. | Every page byte-identical. |

The upstream suite and the fuzzers compare output byte for byte, and they also compare the
type and message of any error a template raises.

## What's identical

- **The template language**: TAL, METAL, i18n, `${...}`, every expression type, and
  whitespace and attribute handling, down to the byte.
- **The Python API**: the template classes and their options, `PageTemplateLoader`, macros,
  `translate` functions, `tal:on-error` handlers, and `CHAMELEON_*` environment variables.
- **The modules**: `chameleon_rs.compat.install()` maps each Chameleon module to the
  chameleon-rs module of the same name.
- **Errors**: the same exception types, and the same formatted messages with the template
  position and expression.
- **The helper libraries**: the APIs of chameleon_partials, chameleon-flask, fastapi-chameleon
  and chameleon-robyn, built in.

## Known differences

These are deliberate. Each comes from chameleon-rs compiling to a native program rather than
to Python source code.

| Area | Chameleon | chameleon-rs |
|---|---|---|
| `template.source` | The generated Python module's code. | With `keep_source=True`, a readable dump of the compiled program. It isn't Python. |
| Custom expression types | A class whose compiler returns Python AST statements. | Supported through a bridge that wraps the AST in a Python function, at the speed of an ordinary Python call. Types that depend on Chameleon's compiler internals beyond that interface aren't supported. |
| `CHAMELEON_CACHE` | Writes the generated modules to disk and loads them on the next start. | Checks the directory but writes nothing. Compiling is about 70x faster than Chameleon, so there's little to cache. |
| Code-generation modules | `chameleon.nodes`, `chameleon.program`, `chameleon.zpt.program`, `chameleon.benchmark`. | Not provided, since chameleon-rs doesn't generate code. Importing them raises `ModuleNotFoundError`. |

### Code blocks

Chameleon compiles `<?python ... ?>` blocks into the template's render function, so what a
block defines is a local of that call. chameleon-rs runs a block in a namespace kept per
template and render, which differs in two ways:

- **Recursive partials share it.** Two frames of the same template in one render (a partial
  that renders itself) see each other's block definitions, where each Chameleon call has its
  own.
- **`default` and `attrs` inside a block** are ordinary names. Chameleon aliases them there as
  in expressions (the default marker and the element's attributes).

### `render_partial` in `econtext`

With chameleon_partials, `render_partial` is a model value, so it shows up in the template's
`econtext` and in the argument list of a render error. The built-in `render_partial` is a
builtin of every template, so it is not in either.

### Corner cases in slot bodies

Three cases, all involving the slot fills of a macro call together with `tal:on-error` or
i18n settings, render differently. No real template we've seen does this; each is pinned by a
test that fails if the behaviour changes.

- **A failing expression under a handler in a slot body** whose slot sits inside
  `i18n:translate` or `i18n:name`. Chameleon writes a text node
  and its expressions as one piece, so when an expression fails, the text before it in the
  same node is dropped with it. chameleon-rs writes that text first, so it stays
  (`<q>Q` where Chameleon gives `<q>`).
- **A handler on an `i18n:name` element** whose content calls a macro that fails partway: the
  same difference, for the text of the failing node inside the macro.
- **A fill no macro took**, used by a later macro call while the calling template has
  different `i18n:domain`, `i18n:context` or `i18n:target` settings: values converted by that
  fill use the settings where it was defined. Chameleon uses the settings at the later call.

### Behaviour of the helper libraries

The built-ins differ from chameleon_partials, chameleon-flask, fastapi-chameleon and
chameleon-robyn in a few ways that don't affect templates that worked before:

- **Partial paths.** A path that isn't in the configured template folder is also looked for
  next to the calling template, where chameleon_partials would raise.
  `configure(partial_search='registered')` restores the original lookup. See
  [Partials](partials.qmd#how-a-path-is-found).
- **Async views await model values.** An async view renders with `render_async`, so a model
  value that is awaitable (a coroutine, task or future, or a test double such as
  `AsyncMock()`) is awaited where the template uses it. The original libraries rendered the
  object itself.
- **Setup.** Every `configure()` call applies (`register_extensions` ignored later calls), and
  `configure(..., app=app)` checks the decorator order at startup.

### `render_async` and a replaced `render`

`render_async()` honours a `render()` that a subclass overrides, since the override may add
defaults or post-process the output: it calls it, synchronously, so awaitable values are not
awaited. Assigning a new function to `PageTemplate.render` (a monkeypatch, for example to time
renders) counts as such an override. Every `render_async()`, including the async views of the
framework integrations, then renders synchronously through your function. See
[Migrating](migrating.qmd#timing-renders) for a way to time both.

## Found a difference?

If a template renders differently on chameleon-rs than on Chameleon, that's a bug. Please
[open an issue](https://github.com/mikeckennedy/chameleon-rust/issues) with the template, the
model, and both outputs. [Shadow mode](switching-from-chameleon.qmd#check-your-own-app-first-shadow-mode)
can find such templates in a running app.
